business: a Gauteng based FMCG distributor selling to Modern Trade, General Trade, Wholesale and HoReCa customers from three distribution centres
reader: the CFO and the Commercial Director
rules: Twelve month figures and two year figures must never be mixed; say which window a figure covers. Dead stock is working capital, not profit.

sections.gap: The gap: revenue grew, gross profit did not keep up
sections.water: The range sold at a loss (Cascade Springs bottled water, after freight and rebates)
sections.promo: The promotion that loses money (Brightwash Powder 2kg, Buy 2 Get 1 Free)
sections.discount: The discount nobody reset (Summit Cash & Carry)
sections.stock: Sales that never happened (weekend stock-outs at the Gauteng DC)
sections.dead: Stock nobody is buying (discontinued Halo Shine aerosols)

hero.label: of gross profit did not arrive, despite the revenue that should have carried it

findings.title: The range sold at a loss
findings.note: contribution on bottled water, after freight and rebates

findings.title: The promotion that loses money
findings.note: gross profit per case on deal, against R44 off it

findings.title: The discount nobody reset
findings.note: revenue forgone in twelve months on one account

findings.title: Stock nobody is buying
findings.note: of discontinued stock sitting at cost

examples: Which brands lose money after freight and rebates?
How did Summit Cash & Carry's realised discount change by month?
Which products lost the most revenue to weekend stock-outs?
What was gross margin in each of the last six months?

tables.name: mart_gp_bridge
tables.description: The closing visual. Why gross profit grew 4.1% while revenue grew 11.9%, as a bridge from what gross profit would have been had margin held at last year's rate down to what was actually earned. The difference is the gap, and each step is a driver's share of it. Every step covers the same trailing twelve months as the gap, taken from period_end. The promotion and discount steps once summed the whole two year window inside a one year gap, which overstated both and left the residual too small. The residual row, other discount drift and mix, absorbs overlap between the named drivers andâ€¦

columns.name: step_order
columns.description: Position of the step in the bridge, anchor first and actual gross profit last.

columns.name: driver
values: Bulk water taking share at a low margin
Discount creep on the largest account
Gross profit at last year's margin

columns.name: step_type
columns.description: anchor is gross profit at last year's margin, decrease is a driver, total is actual gross profit.

columns.name: effect_zar
columns.description: In rand. For the anchor and the total, a level of gross profit. For a driver, the gross profit it cost over the trailing twelve months, negative because it pulls the bridge down.

columns.name: finding_ref
columns.description: The dashboard section that examines this driver. Empty on the residual, which has no section of its own.

columns.name: pct_of_gap
columns.description: The driver's share of the gap, in percent. Empty on the anchor and the total, which are levels rather than movements. The shares of the four drivers sum to 100.

columns.name: total_gap_zar
columns.description: Gross profit at last year's margin less actual gross profit, the headline the page opens on.

tables.name: mart_margin_waterfall
tables.description: FINDING 1. Feeds the margin waterfall: a chart that walks a brand from revenue down to what it was really worth, one bar at a time - revenue, less cost of goods, to gross profit, then the three costs Meridian records at order level, ending at contribution. One row per period, brand and step of the waterfall, so each row is one bar. Two rolling twelve month periods are provided so the current year can be shown against the one before it. Every row also carries the brand's own totals and margins, so a tooltip or a summary tile needs no second query. The Cascade Springs bulk water range is whatâ€¦

columns.name: period_label
columns.description: Which twelve month window the row covers - "Trailing twelve months" or "Prior twelve months". Both end on the last day of data.

columns.name: period_order
columns.description: Sort key for the period, 1 for the trailing year and 2 for the year before it.

columns.name: period_start
columns.description: First day included in the period.

columns.name: period_end
columns.description: Last day included in the period.

columns.name: brand
columns.description: The brand the waterfall is drawn for. Brand is the level at which a range decision is actually taken.

columns.name: category
columns.description: The merchandising category the brand sits in.

columns.name: is_bulk_water
columns.description: True for the Cascade Springs range. Filter on this to go straight to finding 1.

columns.name: step_order
columns.description: Position of the bar in the waterfall, 1 through 7. Sort on this to draw the chart in the right order.

columns.name: step_label
columns.description: The name of the bar - Revenue, Cost of goods sold, Gross profit, Allocated freight, Allocated handling, Allocated customer rebate, Net contribution.

columns.name: step_type
columns.description: Whether the bar is a running subtotal that sits on the axis ("total") or a movement from the bar before it ("delta"). Waterfall charts draw the two differently.

columns.name: step_value_zar
columns.description: The value of this bar in rand, already signed the way it should be drawn - costs are negative so they step the chart downward.

columns.name: running_total_zar
columns.description: Where the waterfall stands after this step, in rand. This is the height the bar reaches. On the last step it equals net contribution.

columns.name: step_pct_of_revenue
columns.description: This step as a percentage of the brand's revenue for the period. Makes the size of the freight and rebate steps comparable across brands of very different sizes.

columns.name: units
columns.description: Packs sold of the brand in the period, net of returns.

columns.name: sales_line_count
columns.description: Number of order lines the brand appeared on in the period. A sense of how widely the range is bought, rather than how much of it.

columns.name: revenue_zar
columns.description: The brand's invoiced revenue for the period after discount, in rand.

columns.name: cogs_zar
columns.description: What the goods sold cost Meridian to buy, in rand.

columns.name: gross_profit_zar
columns.description: Revenue less cost of goods, in rand. The number the business currently manages by.

columns.name: allocated_freight_zar
columns.description: The brand's share of delivery costs, shared out by the weight it put on trucks. In rand.

columns.name: allocated_handling_zar
columns.description: The brand's share of warehouse picking and packing costs, shared out by the number of order lines. In rand.

columns.name: allocated_rebate_zar
columns.description: The brand's share of volume rebates paid back to customers, shared out by revenue. In rand.

columns.name: contribution_zar
columns.description: Gross profit less freight, handling and rebate - what the brand was actually worth for the period, in rand. Negative means the range destroyed value.

columns.name: weight_kg
columns.description: Total kilograms of the brand shipped in the period. The reason the freight step is the size it is.

columns.name: brand_gross_margin_pct
columns.description: Gross profit as a percentage of revenue. The margin the business quotes today.

columns.name: brand_contribution_margin_pct
columns.description: Contribution as a percentage of revenue. The margin the business should be quoting. The gap between this and gross margin is the whole finding.

columns.name: revenue_per_kg_zar
columns.description: Rand of revenue earned per kilogram shipped. A measure of value density - the lower it is, the more of the delivery cost the range swallows relative to what it brings in, and the more likely it is to be unprofitable once freight is honestly charged.

columns.name: is_margin_trap
columns.description: True where the brand shows a positive gross profit and a negative contribution for the period. In other words, the range looks profitable in today's reporting and is losing money in reality.

tables.name: mart_promo_performance
tables.description: FINDING 2. Feeds the promotion chart: units, revenue and profit week by week for every SKU that has ever been promoted, with each week labelled by what was happening to it. One row per SKU, trading week and promotion phase. A week produces one row normally, and two only where a promotion starts or ends part way through it - in which case the two parts are reported separately rather than averaged into a number that describes neither. The mart answers two questions from the same rows. First, the straight comparison: group by promotion phase and look at profit per unit on promotion againstâ€¦

columns.name: sku
columns.description: The promoted product.

columns.name: product_name
columns.description: Full trade description of the product.

columns.name: brand
columns.description: Brand of the product.

columns.name: category
columns.description: Merchandising category of the product.

columns.name: subcategory
columns.description: Merchandising segment of the product.

columns.name: week_start_date
columns.description: The Monday the trading week begins on. Meridian does not trade on Sundays, so a Monday-start week contains exactly the trading days of a promotion window and the shaded promotion blocks line up cleanly with the weeks on the chart.

columns.name: year_month
columns.description: The month the week starts in, as "2026-08". For rolling a weekly chart up to a monthly one.

columns.name: promo_phase
columns.description: What was happening to the SKU that week. "On promotion" means a promotion was live. "Post-promotion (4 weeks)" covers the four weeks straight after a window closed, which is where pantry loading shows up. "Baseline" is ordinary trading, neither on promotion nor in the shadow of one. Where a live promotion overlapsâ€¦

columns.name: is_on_promo_week
columns.description: True where the phase is "On promotion". A convenience flag for shading the chart.

columns.name: promo_id
columns.description: Identifier of the promotion that put the week into its phase, whether the promotion was running or had just ended.

columns.name: promo_name
columns.description: Name of that promotion, for example "Brightwash Buy 2 Get 1 Free - Q3".

columns.name: mechanic
columns.description: How the promotion works - a percentage off, a multibuy, or a buy-two-get-one-free. The mechanic determines the effective discount, and a buy-two-get-one-free is a third off however it is described internally.

columns.name: funding_source
columns.description: Who pays for the promotion, either "Supplier co-funded" or "Meridian funded". Note that co-funded does not mean free.

columns.name: planned_discount_pct
columns.description: The discount the promotion was designed to give, on a 0 to 100 scale. Worth holding next to realised discount, which is what customers actually received.

columns.name: sales_line_count
columns.description: Number of order lines for the SKU in the week. A read on how many customers bought, as opposed to how much they bought.

columns.name: units
columns.description: Packs of the SKU sold in the week, net of returns. The series that makes the promotion spike and the hangover trough visible.

columns.name: gross_value_zar
columns.description: What the week's volume would have billed at full price before discount, in rand.

columns.name: discount_value_zar
columns.description: The rand value of discount given in the week - gross value less revenue.

columns.name: revenue_zar
columns.description: Invoiced revenue for the SKU in the week after discount, in rand.

columns.name: cogs_zar
columns.description: Cost of the goods sold in the week, in rand.

columns.name: gross_profit_zar
columns.description: Revenue less cost of goods for the week, in rand. On Brightwash promotion weeks this is negative, which is the finding in one number.

columns.name: contribution_zar
columns.description: Gross profit for the week less the week's share of freight, handling and rebate, in rand. The full picture of what the week was worth.

columns.name: gross_margin_pct
columns.description: Gross profit as a percentage of revenue for the week.

columns.name: realised_discount_pct
columns.description: The discount customers actually received in the week, as a percentage - discount value over gross value. This is what was really given away, which is not always what the promotion planned.

columns.name: gp_per_unit_zar
columns.description: Gross profit divided by packs sold, in rand per pack. The cleanest way to compare a promotion week with a normal week, because it strips out the fact that a promotion week sells far more volume.

columns.name: revenue_per_unit_zar
columns.description: Revenue divided by packs sold, in rand per pack. The effective price achieved.

columns.name: baseline_units_per_week
columns.description: What this SKU sells in an average normal week, calculated from its own baseline weeks only. Using the SKU's own history keeps seasonality, channel mix and price out of the comparison.

columns.name: baseline_gp_per_unit_zar
columns.description: Gross profit per pack in normal trading for this SKU, in rand. The rate promoted volume would have earned had it been sold at ordinary prices.

columns.name: baseline_revenue_per_unit_zar
columns.description: Revenue per pack in normal trading for this SKU, in rand. The effective everyday price.

columns.name: baseline_gross_margin_pct
columns.description: Gross margin percentage in normal trading for this SKU. Put this next to the promotion's discount - when the discount exceeds the margin, every promoted pack loses money.

columns.name: volume_index_vs_baseline_pct
columns.description: The week's volume as a percentage of a normal week. 100 is normal. Promotion weeks run well above it, and the four weeks after a window closes sit well below it - around 45 for Brightwash, meaning less than half of normal trading. This single column is the pantry-loading hangover.

columns.name: gp_forgone_vs_baseline_zar
columns.description: Profit given up on the week's volume, in rand - the week's packs valued at the difference between normal profit per pack and what they actually earned. Positive means the week earned less than the same volume would have in normal trading. Summed across a promotion's weeks it is the true cost of running it.

columns.name: units_below_baseline
columns.description: How many packs short of a normal week the week fell, floored at zero. Most meaningful on post-promotion weeks, where it measures the volume that was pulled forward into the promotion rather than created by it.

tables.name: mart_discount_trend
tables.description: FINDING 3. Feeds a two-line chart: the discount a customer group is actually getting month by month, against what the rest of its channel is getting. One line climbs steadily and the other is flat. One row per customer group, channel and calendar month. "Realised" is the operative word. Nobody ever approved a fifteen and a half percent discount for Summit Cash & Carry, Meridian's largest account. It arrived one concession at a time over two years, was never reviewed and never reset, and it is invisible on any single branch or in any single month. It only appears when the branches are addedâ€¦

columns.name: customer_group
columns.description: The parent business, with branches rolled together. This is the level at which the pricing relationship actually exists, even though every branch invoices separately.

columns.name: channel
columns.description: The group's route to market. Discounts are only comparable within a channel, so the comparison lines are built per channel.

columns.name: year_month
columns.description: The month, as "2026-08". The x axis of the chart.

columns.name: month_start_date
columns.description: First day of the month, for sorting and for date filters.

columns.name: trading_branch_count
columns.description: How many of the group's branches actually placed an order that month. Worth watching, because a change in realised discount can come from mix between branches rather than from any price decision.

columns.name: gross_value_zar
columns.description: What the group's purchases that month would have billed at full price, in rand. The denominator of realised discount.

columns.name: revenue_zar
columns.description: What the group was actually invoiced that month after discount, in rand.

columns.name: discount_value_zar
columns.description: The rand value of discount given to the group that month - gross value less revenue. The real cost of the pricing, in money.

columns.name: realised_discount_pct
columns.description: The discount the group actually received that month, as a percentage of list value. This is the line that climbs from around 8 percent to around 15.5 percent over two years.

columns.name: channel_realised_discount_pct
columns.description: The same measure for the whole channel that month, including this group. The broad comparison.

columns.name: channel_excl_group_realised_discount_pct
columns.description: The same measure for the channel with this group taken out. The fairer comparison for a large account, because a big group otherwise drags the average it is being judged against toward its own number. This is the flat line on the chart.

columns.name: discount_gap_vs_channel_pct_pts
columns.description: How many percentage points more discount the group received than the rest of its channel that month. A positive and widening gap is the signature of discount creep.

columns.name: baseline_month_start_date
columns.description: The first month the group appears in the data - the month its benchmark discount is taken from.

columns.name: baseline_discount_pct
columns.description: The discount the group was realising when it first appears in the data. Used as the benchmark for what should have held if nobody had let it drift.

columns.name: discount_creep_pct_pts
columns.description: Percentage points of discount the group has gained since its own starting point. This is the drift itself, isolated from how much the group buys.

columns.name: revenue_forgone_vs_baseline_zar
columns.description: Money left on the table that month purely because the discount drifted - the extra percentage points applied to the month's list value, in rand. Summed over the period it is what the finding is worth.

columns.name: share_of_channel_revenue_pct
columns.description: The group's revenue that month as a percentage of the whole channel's. Shows how much leverage the account has, which is usually the reason the discount was conceded in the first place.

columns.name: group_total_revenue_zar
columns.description: The group's total revenue across the whole period, in rand. Repeated on every row so the largest accounts can be found or filtered without a second query.

columns.name: group_share_of_company_revenue_pct
columns.description: The group's share of Meridian's total revenue across the whole period, as a percentage. The context that makes a few points of discount drift material.

tables.name: mart_stockout_impact
tables.description: FINDING 4. Puts a number on sales that never happened. One row per SKU per week, for every week in which the Thursday stock count at WH-01 read zero on a line that runs out chronically. Replenishment into WH-01 runs Monday to Wednesday, so the Thursday count is the first honest read on whether the week can be finished. When it reads zero, Friday and Saturday orders for that line cannot be filled. Three Modern Trade hero lines - Meadowvale Full Cream Milk, Sunveld Maize Meal and Softleaf Toilet Tissue - do this in roughly a third of all weeks. None of this appears in a sales report, byâ€¦

columns.name: sku
columns.description: The product that ran out.

columns.name: product_name
columns.description: Full trade description of the product.

columns.name: brand
columns.description: Brand of the product.

columns.name: category
columns.description: Merchandising category of the product.

columns.name: subcategory
columns.description: Merchandising segment of the product.

columns.name: warehouse_code
columns.description: The distribution centre the stock-out was observed at. Always WH-01, the centre whose Monday to Wednesday replenishment cycle causes the pattern.

columns.name: week_start_date
columns.description: The Monday of the week that was lost. Each row is one such week.

columns.name: year_month
columns.description: The month the week falls in, as "2026-08". For rolling the losses up to a monthly total.

columns.name: thursday_snapshot_date
columns.description: The Thursday the stock count read zero.

columns.name: thursday_units_on_hand
columns.description: Packs on hand at that count. Zero by definition on every row in this mart - it is carried so the reader can see the evidence rather than take the flag on trust.

columns.name: baseline_fri_sat_units
columns.description: What this SKU normally ships on a Friday and Saturday together, averaged across the weeks when Thursday stock was not zero. The SKU's own normal weekend, which is the only fair benchmark for what it would have sold.

columns.name: actual_fri_sat_units
columns.description: What actually shipped on the Friday and Saturday of this week. Usually close to nothing, because there was nothing to ship.

columns.name: lost_units_est
columns.description: The estimate of packs not supplied - normal weekend demand less what actually shipped, floored at zero so a week that happened to beat its baseline cannot quietly offset a real loss elsewhere. This is an estimate, and it is deliberately conservative.

columns.name: avg_realised_price_zar
columns.description: What a pack of this SKU actually sells for in Modern Trade, in rand - revenue divided by packs across the whole period. Used rather than list price, because valuing lost sales at list would overstate the loss by the discount that would have been given.

columns.name: avg_gross_profit_per_unit_zar
columns.description: Gross profit a pack of this SKU actually earns in Modern Trade, in rand.

columns.name: lost_revenue_zar
columns.description: Revenue forgone in the week - estimated lost packs at the realised price, in rand. Sum this across all rows for the headline number.

columns.name: lost_gross_profit_zar
columns.description: Gross profit forgone in the week, in rand. The revenue number is what the conversation opens with; this is what the loss was actually worth.

columns.name: thursday_weeks_observed
columns.description: How many Thursday counts exist for this SKU across the whole period. The denominator behind the stock-out rate.

columns.name: stockout_week_count
columns.description: How many of those Thursdays read zero for this SKU.

columns.name: stockout_week_pct
columns.description: The share of Thursdays that read zero, as a percentage. Around 35 for the three hero lines, which is roughly one week in three where the weekend cannot be served.

tables.name: mart_dead_stock
tables.description: FINDING 5. What is sitting in the warehouses that nobody is buying any more. One row per SKU per distribution centre, as at the most recent stock count. Live stock is included alongside dead stock on purpose, so a chart can show the dead pile against the total it is part of rather than as a number with no scale - filter on is_dead_stock for the finding itself. The Halo Shine aerosol range was discontinued and has not sold in over six months, yet eight of its SKUs still hold stock in WH-02. This is a working capital problem rather than a profit one: the cash is already spent, it is simply notâ€¦

columns.name: sku
columns.description: The product held in stock.

columns.name: product_name
columns.description: Full trade description of the product.

columns.name: brand
columns.description: Brand of the product. Dead stock usually arrives a whole brand at a time, because ranges are delisted as ranges.

columns.name: category
columns.description: Merchandising category of the product.

columns.name: subcategory
columns.description: Merchandising segment of the product.

columns.name: status
columns.description: Whether the line is still part of the active range, "Active" or "Discontinued".

columns.name: is_discontinued
columns.description: True where the line has been withdrawn from the range. A discontinued line holding stock is the clearest case of dead stock, because there is no plan that brings it back.

columns.name: warehouse_code
columns.description: The distribution centre holding the stock.

columns.name: warehouse_name
columns.description: Name of that distribution centre, for example "Meridian Coastal DC".

columns.name: warehouse_region
columns.description: The province the distribution centre is in.

columns.name: snapshot_date
columns.description: The date of the stock count this row reports, which is the most recent count in the data.

columns.name: as_of_date
columns.description: The last day the business traded in the data. Days since last sale is measured against this rather than against today, so the figures do not drift as time passes.

columns.name: units_on_hand
columns.description: Packs physically held at that distribution centre at the latest count.

columns.name: units_in_transit
columns.description: Packs still on their way to the distribution centre. On a dead line this is worth checking - it means more of the same is still arriving.

columns.name: unit_cost_zar
columns.description: What Meridian paid its supplier for one pack, in rand.

columns.name: list_price_zar
columns.description: The published trade price of one pack before discount, in rand. Useful for judging how much room there is to clear the stock at a markdown.

columns.name: stock_value_zar
columns.description: What the stock on hand is worth at cost - packs multiplied by unit cost, in rand. This is cash currently tied up, whether the line is alive or dead.

columns.name: avg_weekly_demand_units
columns.description: Average packs of this SKU shipped from this distribution centre per week over the whole period. Near zero on a dead line, which is the point.

columns.name: weeks_cover
columns.description: How many weeks the stock would last at normal demand. Empty where there is no demand at all at that centre, which is the strongest signal of all.

columns.name: last_sale_date
columns.description: The last date the SKU was sold anywhere in the business, counting sales only - a credit note is a customer sending stock back, not evidence the line still moves. Empty where it has never sold.

columns.name: days_since_last_sale
columns.description: Days between the last sale and the last day of trading in the data. Over 180 is the trade's working definition of dead. Empty where the line has never sold.

columns.name: has_ever_sold
columns.description: False where the SKU has no sales history at all. These are the worst cases, since there is no evidence anyone ever wanted the line.

columns.name: lifetime_units_sold
columns.description: Total packs of the SKU ever sold across the whole period. Context for whether a line is genuinely dead or simply slow.

columns.name: is_dead_stock
columns.description: True where there is physical stock on hand and the line has not sold in over 180 days, or has never sold. Six months is the FMCG convention - anything that has not moved in two quarters is not going to move on its own.

columns.name: dead_stock_reason
columns.description: Plain wording of why the row is flagged - "Discontinued and no sale in 180+ days", "No sale in 180+ days" or "Never sold". Empty where the stock is not dead. Written out so it can be dropped straight into a report without being decoded.
values: Discontinued and no sale in 180+ days

columns.name: dead_stock_value_zar
columns.description: The stock value in rand where the row is dead, and zero where it is not. Sum this column to get the working capital that could be released, without needing a filter on the chart.

tables.name: dim_product
tables.description: The product master, one row per SKU. Everything the business knows about a line it sells: what it is called, who makes it, what it weighs, what it costs Meridian to buy and what it is listed at. This is the cleaned version - blank costs have already been filled in upstream and are flagged where that happened, so nobody has to guess whether a margin is real or imputed.

columns.name: sku
columns.description: The stock keeping unit code, for example MP-1016. Unique identifier for a sellable product and the key every sales and stock record points at.

columns.name: product_name
columns.description: The full trade description of the line, brand and pack together, for example "Brightwash Powder 2kg x6". This is what appears on an invoice and what a buyer would recognise.

columns.name: brand
columns.description: The brand the line is sold under, for example "Cascade Springs". Brand is the level at which range decisions are actually taken, so most profitability reporting is grouped here.

columns.name: category
columns.description: Top level merchandising category, for example "Beverages" or "Household Care". Eight categories cover the whole range.

columns.name: subcategory
columns.description: The merchandising segment within the category, for example "Bottled Water" within Beverages. This is the level at which a buyer plans a shelf.

columns.name: pack_size
columns.description: The selling configuration, for example "12x1.5L" - how many units in what size, as the trade quotes it. Meridian sells cases, so a single unit of quantity is one of these packs.

columns.name: weight_kg
columns.description: Gross weight of one selling pack in kilograms. This is the number that drives freight - a delivery is paid for by what it weighs, so weight is how the cost of getting an order to a customer is fairly shared out between the lines on that order.

columns.name: unit_cost_zar
columns.description: What Meridian pays its supplier for one pack, in rand. This is the cost used for gross profit everywhere in the warehouse.

columns.name: unit_cost_is_imputed
columns.description: True where the supplier cost was missing in the source system and has been estimated upstream from the category's normal cost to price relationship. Margins on these lines are indicative rather than exact, and this flag is how you tell which ones.

columns.name: list_price_zar
columns.description: The published trade price of one pack before any customer discount, in rand. The starting point of every price negotiation and the benchmark realised discount is measured against.

columns.name: status
columns.description: Whether the line is still part of the active range, either "Active" or "Discontinued".

columns.name: is_discontinued
columns.description: True where the line has been withdrawn from the range. Discontinued lines can still hold stock in a warehouse long after the last sale, which is the whole of finding 5.

columns.name: launch_date
columns.description: The date the line was first listed for sale.

columns.name: is_bulk_water
columns.description: True for the Cascade Springs range, which is Meridian's entire bulk bottled water offer. Flagged because this range behaves unlike anything else in the portfolio: it is very heavy relative to its value, so it consumes far more of a delivery's cost than its share of revenue suggests. It is the subject of finding 1.

tables.name: dim_customer
tables.description: The trading account master, one row per customer, with the sales representative who owns the relationship attached and the account rolled up to its parent group. The grouping is the important part: large customers trade through several branches under separate account numbers, and pricing decisions that look small on one branch are substantial once the branches are added together. Finding 3 is invisible without it.

columns.name: customer_id
columns.description: The account number, for example CUS-5041. Unique identifier for a trading account and the key sales records point at.

columns.name: customer_name
columns.description: The account name exactly as the business uses it, including the branch marker - for example "Summit Cash & Carry Depot".

columns.name: customer_group
columns.description: The parent business the account belongs to, derived by stripping one trailing branch marker from the account name. Meridian uses two branch conventions: numbered banners such as "Baywater Market #03", and named depots such as "Summit Cash & Carry Depot", "... Branch" and "... Hub" - all three of which roll up toâ€¦

columns.name: channel
columns.description: The route to market the account trades through - Modern Trade, General Trade, Wholesale or HoReCa. Channel drives almost everything about how an account behaves - order size, discount level, what it buys and how much rebate it earns.

columns.name: region
columns.description: The province the account trades in. Region determines which distribution centre serves it and therefore what the delivery costs.

columns.name: city
columns.description: The town or city the account is located in.

columns.name: credit_terms_days
columns.description: How many days after invoice the account has agreed to pay, for example 30. A commercial term, not a payment record.

columns.name: rebate_pct
columns.description: The volume rebate rate agreed with the account, as a decimal fraction of what they spend (0.06 means six percent). This is money handed back after the sale, so it never appears in the invoiced price and is easy to forget when judging whether an account is profitable.

columns.name: onboarded_date
columns.description: The date the account first started trading with Meridian.

columns.name: rep_id
columns.description: Identifier of the sales representative who owns the account.

columns.name: rep_name
columns.description: Name of the sales representative who owns the account.

columns.name: rep_team
columns.description: The team the representative belongs to, either "Trade Sales" or "Key Accounts".

columns.name: rep_region
columns.description: The territory the representative covers. Usually the same as the customer's region, and worth checking where it is not.

columns.name: is_group_branch
columns.description: True where the account is one branch of a multi-branch group, false where it is a standalone business. Use it to separate chain trade from independent trade.
